questions.q: A program accepts a percentage from 0 to 100. Sort each test value by the kind of data it is.
questions.feedback: Boundary data is on the limit, invalid data is the right type and out of range, erroneous data is the wrong type altogether.

questions.q: Explain why testing a program with normal data only is not enough.

markPoints.concept: normal data is what the program was written to expect
accept: expect|expected|expects|sensible|designed for|meant to handle|supposed to|everyday|written for|designed around|built for
markPoints.exemplar: Normal data is exactly what the program was written to expect.

markPoints.concept: so faults only appear when something unexpected or on the limit is entered
markPoints.exemplar: This means a fault only shows up when something on the limit or of the wrong type is entered.

questions.example: Normal data is what the program was written to handle, so it will almost always work. The faults live at the edges: a value exactly on the limit, a number just outside the range, or a word where a number was expected. Testing only with sensible input finds none of them.
questions.paraphrase: Since ordinary values are the ones the program was designed around, problems only surface with input at the boundary or of entirely the wrong kind.
questions.feedback: What normal data proves, and where the faults actually are.

questions.q: A program accepts a mark from 0 to 50. Which of these is erroneous data?
questions.feedback: Erroneous data is the wrong data type. 51 and -1 are numbers in the wrong range, which makes them invalid rather than erroneous.

questions.feedback: Good test data includes the awkward cases. A value chosen because it works tests nothing.
